title: Continuity and the Intermediate Value Theorem

questions.q: State the three conditions that must all hold for $f$ to be continuous at $x=a$.
Determine whether $f(x)=\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ (for $x\neq2$, with $f(2)=4$ defined separately) is continuous at $x=2$.
questions.answer: $\lim_{x\to2}f(x) = \lim_{x\to2}(x+2)=4$. Since $f(2)=4$ matches, all three conditions hold: $f$ is continuous at $x=2$.

Classify the discontinuity of each function at the indicated point:
answers: Jump — the floor function steps from $1$ to $2$.

questions.q: Show that $f(x)=x^3-3x+1$ has a root in $(0,1)$, using the IVT.
questions.answer: $f(0)=1>0$ and $f(1)=1-3+1=-1<0$. Since $f$ is continuous (a polynomial) and changes sign on $[0,1]$, the IVT guarantees a root in $(0,1)$.

questions.q: A continuous function $g$ satisfies $g(1)=-3$ and $g(5)=7$. Explain why $g$ must take the value $0$ somewhere in $[1,5]$, and state the theorem used.
questions.answer: By the IVT, since $g$ is continuous on $[1,5]$ and $0$ lies between $g(1)=-3$ and $g(5)=7$, there must exist some $c\in[1,5]$ with $g(c)=0$.

questions.q: A cup of coffee's temperature (in $°$C) is a continuous function of time, starting at $90°$C and cooling to $25°$C over 30 minutes. Explain, using the IVT, why the coffee must have been exactly $50°$C at some point.
questions.answer: Temperature is a continuous function of time; since $50$ lies between the starting value $90$ and ending value $25$, the IVT guarantees the temperature equaled $50°$C at some instant during the 30 minutes.

questions.q: Determine the largest interval(s) on which $f(x)=\sqrt{9-x^2}$ is continuous.
questions.answer: The expression under the square root must be non-negative: $9-x^2\geq0 \Rightarrow -3\leq x\leq3$. $f$ is continuous on the closed interval $[-3,3]$.

questions.q: Determine all values of $x$ where $f(x)=\frac{x+1}{x^2-x-6}$ is discontinuous, and classify each discontinuity.
questions.answer: Factor denominator: $x^2-x-6=(x-3)(x+2)$. Discontinuities at $x=3$ and $x=-2$. Since the numerator $x+1$ shares no common factor, both are infinite (vertical asymptote) discontinuities, not removable.

sections.heading: Using the IVT to approximate roots

questions.q: Show that $f(x)=\cos x-x$ has a root in $(0,1)$, then use the IVT with the midpoint to narrow the interval to a length-$0.5$ subinterval.
questions.answer: $f(0)=\cos0-0=1>0$. $f(1)=\cos1-1\approx0.540-1=-0.460<0$. Sign change confirms a root exists in $(0,1)$. Midpoint $x=0.5$: $f(0.5)=\cos(0.5)-0.5\approx0.878-0.5=0.378>0$. Since $f(0.5)>0$ and $f(1)<0$, the root lies in $(0.5,1)$.

questions.q: The graph shows $f(x)=\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ for $x\neq2$, simplifying to $f(x)=x+2$. Use the graph to describe what would need to be true of $f(2)$ for the function to be continuous there.
questions.answer: For continuity at $x=2$, we would need $f(2)$ to be defined and equal to the limit, $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)=4$. Since the original expression is undefined at $x=2$ (a hole in the graph at $(2,4)$), defining $f(2)=4$ would remove the discontinuity.

sections.heading: Continuity of piecewise and combined functions

questions.q: Determine whether $f(x)=|x-3|$ is continuous at $x=3$, checking all three conditions.
questions.answer: $f(3)=0$ is defined. $\lim_{x\to3^-}f(x)=\lim_{x\to3^-}(3-x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to3^+}f(x)=\lim_{x\to3^+}(x-3)=0$, so $\lim_{x\to3}f(x)=0$. Since $\lim_{x\to3}f(x)=0=f(3)$, $f$ is continuous at $x=3$ (even though it has a corner there, which affects differentiability, not continuity).

questions.q: If $f$ and $g$ are both continuous at $x=a$, explain why $f(x)+g(x)$ and $f(x)\cdot g(x)$ must also be continuous at $x=a$, citing the relevant limit laws.
questions.answer: By the sum and product limit laws, $\lim_{x\to a}[f(x)+g(x)]=\lim_{x\to a}f(x)+\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=f(a)+g(a)$, and similarly $\lim_{x\to a}[f(x)g(x)]=f(a)g(a)$. Since each limit equals the function value at $a$, both the sum and product are continuous at $x=a$.

questions.q: A hiker's elevation (in meters) is a continuous function of distance walked, starting at $200$ m and ending at $850$ m after $5$ km. Explain, using the IVT, why the hiker must have been at exactly $500$ m at some point, and state why this reasoning would fail if elevation were not continuous.
questions.answer: Since elevation is continuous over the 5 km hike, and $500$ lies between the starting value $200$ and ending value $850$, the IVT guarantees some distance $c\in[0,5]$ where elevation equals exactly $500$ m. If elevation could jump discontinuously (e.g. teleporting), the function could skip over $500$ m entirely without ever equaling it.

sections.heading: Continuity with absolute value and radical functions

questions.q: Determine the domain (and hence largest interval of continuity) of $f(x)=\sqrt{x^2-4}$.
questions.answer: Need $x^2-4\geq0$, i.e. $x^2\geq4$, so $x\leq-2$ or $x\geq2$. $f$ is continuous on $(-\infty,-2]\cup[2,\infty)$.

For $f(x)=x^3-4x+1$, evaluate $f(2)$ and $f(3)$, and state whether the IVT guarantees a root in $(2,3)$.
choices: $f(2)=1$, $f(3)=16$ — same sign, but a root is still guaranteed since $f$ is a polynomial.
$f(2)=1$, $f(3)=16$ — same sign, so the IVT does not guarantee a root in $(2,3)$.
$f(2)=1$, $f(3)=16$ — the IVT cannot be applied since $f$ is not continuous.
$f(2)=1$, $f(3)=16$ — opposite signs, so the IVT guarantees a root in $(2,3)$.
questions.answer: $f(x)$ is a polynomial, hence continuous everywhere. $f(2)=1$, $f(3)=16$ — same sign, so the IVT does not guarantee a root in $(2,3)$.
